If i understood Piet correctly,

1. conditioned on col(4) (e..g /NOTIFY) compute
 a) mean, max,min for each of columns 2,9 and 10

Then what we can do in one pass with RHIPE is compute

1. conditioned on col(4) (e..g /NOTIFY) compute
 a) **# of obs**, sum, max,min for each of columns 2,9 and 10

(note, not the mean) You'd have to compute the mean in another pass (which shouldn't require RHIPE).

Here's the code - tested on a file. I dont use rhipe.current.state and neither should others - if a key has few rows it might never be called!
Note
1.  the           ,zips    = "/user/sguha/Rfolder.tar.gz" is not rquired, i need it for my cluster (no R on nodes)
2. the file foo.txt can be found here http://people.mozilla.com:~/sguha/foo.txt
  - download it and place in the HDFS

Hope it helps
Saptarshi

map <- expression({
  tryCatch({
    rows <- do.call('rbind',strsplit(unlist(map.values)," +"))

    apply(rows[,c(4,2,9,10)], 1, function(r){

      nv <- as.numeric(r[2:4])
      for(i in seq_along(nv)){
        rhcollect(list(r[1],col.id <http://col.id>=i), list(count=1, sum=nv[i], max=nv[i],min=nv[i]))

      }
    })
  },error=function(e){
    rhstatus(sprintf("ERROR: Read : %s", e$message))

    rhcounter("R_ERRORS",as.character(e), 1)

  })
})

reduce <- expression(
    pre={

      counts <- 0 ; sums <- 0; mins <- Inf;maxs <- -Inf;
      getName <- function(lst,nm) unlist(lapply(lst,function(j) j[[nm]]))
    }
    ,reduce={
      counts <- counts + sum(getName(reduce.values,"count") )
      sums   <- sums   + sum(getName(reduce.values,"sum") )
      maxs   <- max( c(maxs,getName(reduce.values,"max")) )
      mins   <- min( c(mins,getName(reduce.values,"min")) )
    }
    ,post={
      ## We have no idea if this the last reduce$post for this key ...
      ## So we cannot output a mean ...
      rhcollect(reduce.key, list(count=counts,sum=sums,max=maxs,min=mins))
    }
    )

        rhcollect(reduce.key, c(sums/counts,max=maxs,min=mins))

messages.body_plain:
Hello, everyone.

Below, I am doing a very simple nonparametric bootstrap to approximate the sampling distribution of the sample mean for 30 standard normal random variates. First, I generate the data, and then in 'boot_idx', I store the bootstrap indices for each replication. So, I could pass the data itself around, but I'm choosing to only pass the indices around to keep things simple as my data gets more complex.

When I run the code, I get the following error each time the Map expression is called:

Error in mean(normal_data[v]) : object 'normal_data' not found

Question: How do I export the 'normal_data' object to the individual nodes that run the Map code? One thought was to save 'normal_data' to an RData file and then use the 'shared' argument in the 'rhmr' function to read the data. This doesn't seem like the best approach though.

# Start of Code

# Function to make append parent directory to path
hadoop_dir <- function(path) {
  paste("/home/ramey/rhipe_test/hadoop_data", path, sep = "/")
}

set.seed(42)
bootstrap_reps <- 50
n <- 30
normal_data <- rnorm(n)

boot_idx <- lapply(seq_len(bootstrap_reps), function(k) {
  list(k = k, v = sample(n, replace = TRUE))
})

rhwrite(boot_idx, hadoop_dir("bootstrap_indices"), N = bootstrap_reps)

map_boot <- expression({
   mapply(function(k, v) {
      rhcollect(k, mean(normal_data[v]))
   }, map.keys, map.values)
})

z <- rhmr(map=map_boot,
   ifolder=hadoop_dir("bootstrap_indices"),
   ofolder=hadoop_dir("approx_sampling_distribution"),
   inout=c("sequence", "sequence")
)
rhex(z)

#End of Code

Any thoughts?

Thanks.

John Ramey

I think you only have the two choices you mentioned:

1. Store the data along with the indices for each bootstrap sample -
or if you are doing it this way, you might as well just store the
bootstrap sample itself.

2. Save it as .Rdata and use the shared argument to read it in.

I think #2 is by far the better choice.  What was it about this
approach didn't sound good?

Another thing to consider is generating the indices inside the map and
having no input data.  This approach is useful especially when you are
looking at generating a very large number of samples/runs and the sets
of indices becomes too big.  You need to be careful about getting
independent random number streams if you do it this way, though, and
I'm not an expert on this.

For this, what you could do is set up a vector of random seeds and
save these along with your data and load them in using the shared
argument.  In rhmr, you can specify the input type in the "inout"
argument to be "lapply".  If you do this along with specifying an
argument "N" to be the length of the vector of seeds, this will create
a list of map.values that are the integers along your sequence of
seeds.  Then in the map you can set the seed and generate.  I don't
know  if this is correct but I know others have done it this way and I
think I have in the past.

Another alternative to check into would be the rsprng package
http://rwiki.sciviews.org/doku.php?id=packages:cran:rsprng or rstream
http://math.la.asu.edu/~eubank/webpage/rngStreamPaper.pdf.  Stuff like
this should eventually be built-in.  Others on the list probably know
more about this.

Here's some untested code that could do the trick, supposing you have
a way to generate a sequence of nice seeds that will produce
indpendent random number sequences.

save(normal_data, random_seed_sequence, file="rhipeinput.Rdata")
rhput("rhipeinput.Rdata", "/tmp/rhipeinput.Rdata")

setup <- expression({
   load("rhipeinput.Rdata")
})

map_boot <- expression({
   lapply(map.values, function(x) {
      set.seed(random_seed_sequence[x])
      ind <- sample(30, replace=TRUE)
      rhcollect(x, mean(normal_data[ind]))
   })
})

z <- rhmr(
   map=map_boot,
   inout=c("lapply", "sequence"),
   N=length(random_seed_sequence),
   ofolder=hadoop_dir("approx_sampling_distribution"),
   setup=setup,
   shared="/tmp/rhipeinput.Rdata"
)

I didn't mention this, but when Saptarshi said, "Have the data come
from the map in the same shape", I realized that was the simple way to
go about this, and wished I could draw that out.

Several days went by and today I found myself having to write a simple
test for the combiner, and I decided to base one of the test on this
use case of extracting summary statistics from an nxp matrix divided
up into m chunks on your HDFS.

I uploaded the script as an example of how to approach this problem
here:  https://gist.github.com/2070099

It is adaptable to your problem.  The main parts that would need
altering is what happens in the map prior to calling emit.summary.

The use of this combiner is space efficient.  Essentially the summary
statistics are recombined at least 4 times.  Once per a reduce$reduce
in the combiner, once per a reduce$post in the combiner, once per a
reduce$reduce in the actual reduce, and once per a reduce$post in the
actual reduce.  Each time the shape of the data stays the same, so the
same function can be reapplied to the input.

# REGARDING RANDOM VARIABLES #

I have always been told that if you have unique integer seeds for
Marsenne-Twister then you can treat the samples as independent;
though, I have never researched the literature myself.  It is from
that point of view that I continue.

Here is my approach built on that idea: define a 1 to 1 mapping
between your parameter space crossed with runs unto a subset of the
integers and use that 1 to 1 mapping for the seed.

Usually this takes the form of reserving certain digits of a base 10
number to mapping of certain parameters.  That works as long as your
crossing doesn't get so big that it overruns what a Marsenne-Twister
accepts as a unique seed.  It is a little more work, but each run of
your simulation has a specific seed a priori.

For simulations without parameters you just have runs so use the v in
map.values after input lappply.  For simulations with parameters I
usually end up doing something like this:  I "expand.grid: to form a
parameter space X run crossing of variables (in this snippet "key")
and then map the rows to integers in a way that is 1 to 1

for(i in 1:nrow(key)){
			k = key[i,]
			new.key = k
			new.key$set.seed = k$convolution + 10^2*k$utilization + 10^3*k$rate
+ 10^5*k$run + 10^7*k$convolution.run
			rhcollect(new.key, TRUE)
}

I personally did this as a map.reduce job with 1 map KeyValue pair
then another map follows along and begins the simulation with the
set.seed in the key.  run was actually a parameter from another
simulation and convolution.run was the runs for this situation.  I
made it the high order part of the seed so I could add runs in an
obvious way in the future.

It has the added perk of not needing any details about MapReduce or
Hadoop to be explained when you tell people about the uniqueness of
seeds.  It is language neutral.  It just takes more time, but this is
an aspect of simulation that deserves to take more time.

#  REGARDING VARIABLES MOVING FROM LOCAL R TO MapReduce R #

Regarding moving variables around, I agree with both the OP, Ryan, and
I think we can make it easier to move temp variables to jobs.  I think
Ryan's idea of a temp .Rdata file is do able and reasonably robust. I
think I can implement it.

messages.body_plain:
A quick and dirty 'macro' can be used to export variables (small variables  - small in byte size, so multi megabyte matrices).
My code often is of the form

expression({
BEFORE
mapply(F, 1:length(map.values), map.keys,map.values)
AFTER
})

where F does something. Sometimes i need some code before the mapply, and sometimes after. So i wrote ewrap 'macro' and is called like

m=ewrap({
   rhcollect( list(k,r),1)
})

rhmr(map=m,...)

But this doesn'r do variable export, for that i have rhmr2 which is called as

m=ewrap({
  if(runif(1) < prob1 and runif(1) < prob2)
   do-something
})

rhmr2(map=m, reduce...., params=lis(prob1=prob1,var2=var2,.do-something=function(...) ..., and so on) )

the code for rhmr2 is at the end of the email.

ewrap <- function(co1=NULL,before=NULL,after=NULL,trap=FALSE){
  co <- substitute(co1); before=substitute(before)
  err <- if(trap) function(e) rhcounter("R_ERRORS",as.character(e),1) else function(e) rhcounter("R_UNTRAPPED_ERRORS",as.character(e),1)
  as.expression(bquote({
    .(BE)
    result <- mapply(function(.index,k,r){
      tryCatch(
               .(CO)
               ,error=.(TRAP))
  },1:length(map.values),map.values,map.keys)
    .(AF)
},list(CO=co,BE=before,AF=after,TRAP=err)))
}

rhmr2 <- function(params=NULL,...){
  msetup <- expression({
    if(!is.null(Sys.getenv("param.names"))){
      param.names <- strsplit(Sys.getenv("param.names"),",")[[1]]
      for(x in param.names){
        assign(x, unserialize(charToRaw(Sys.getenv(x))),.GlobalEnv)
      }
    }
  })
  z <- list(...)
  if(!is.null(z$setup)){
    z$setup$map <- c(msetup,z$setup$map)
  } else z$setup=list(map=msetup)
  z$inout <- c('seq','seq')
  f <- list(param.names = paste(names(params),collapse=","))
  for(x in seq_along(params)) f[[ names(params)[[x]] ]] <- rawToChar(serialize(params[[x]],NULL,ascii=TRUE))
  z$mapred <- append(z$mapred, f)
  if(is.null(z$combine))
    if(!is.null(z$reduce)) z$combiner <- TRUE else z$combiner <- FALSE
  do.call(rhmr,z)
}

A real example. I need to compute quantiles of "CYCLE_COLLECTOR" from a JSON data structure stored as R lists.

map <- ewrap({
  if(runif(1)<0.1){
    buildid <- r$info$appBuildID
    variable <- r$histograms[[myname]]$values
    if(is.null(variable)) return(NULL)
    values.raw <- as.numeric(names(variable))
    values.count <- variable
    dd <- data.frame(raw =values.raw[ values.count >0 ],count=values.count[ values.count >0 ])
    dd <- dd[dd$raw>0,]
    dd <- dd[order(dd$raw),]
    if(trim.pct>0){
      cuts <- with(dd,wtd.quantile(raw,count,probs=c(trim.pct,1-trim.pct)))
      dd.2 <- dd[dd$raw> cuts[1] & dd$raw<cuts[2],,drop=FALSE]
      if(nrow(dd.2)>0) dd <- dd.2
    }
    if(nrow(dd)==0) return()
    if(is.function(myTransform))
      dd$raw <- myTransform(dd$raw)
    summary <- with(dd,F(raw, count))
    version <- sapply(r$info$appVersion,function(k) {
      if(grepl("^10",k)) 10 else if (grepl("^11",k)) 11 else if (grepl("^12",k)) 12 else 9
    })
    rhcollect(runif(1), list(id=buildid,version=version ,value=summary))
  }
},trap=TRUE,before={ suppressMessages(library(Hmisc))})

messages.subject: It is hard to underestimate the value of as.expression(bquote({...})) to the Rhipe user.
messages.subject_clean: It is hard to underestimate the value of as.expression(bquote({...})) to the Rhipe user.
messages.body_plain:
It is hard to underestimate the value of things like

map=as.expression(bquote({...}))

For example see:
https://github.com/saptarshiguha/RHIPE/blob/unstable.0.68/standalone_examples/unit_test/unit_test.bquote.make.words.R

In that one, I use the pattern:

	map.args = list(MU.LETTERS=MU.LETTERS, MU.WORDS=MU.WORDS,
make.line=make.line)
		param = list()
		param$map <- as.expression(bquote({
			args = .(map.args)
			attach(args)
			for(v in map.values){
				set.seed(v)
				rhcollect(v,make.line(MU.LETTERS,MU.WORDS))
			}
			detach(args)
		}))

Which is just a really general and clean way to get arguments from
outside of a map expression into a map expression at the time of it is
created in R.  It is also nice when done by hand because you can
review what bquote did simply by printing out the map expression in
the console.

I only mention because the back quote paradigm never made it into the
first generation of documentation, but it is tremendously useful to
the Rhipe user.  As far as I can figure someone discovered its value
and taught the Rhipe users about it several months ago.  I just
learned about bquote this weekend while I was reviewing the new rhwrap
and the make words example.

Awesome stuff.  Thanks to who ever figured that out.

Jeremiah
